newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Tutu rejects de Klerk apartheid evidence.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Tutu rejects de Klerk apartheid evidence.

text.p: South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu launched an emotional attack on F.W. de Klerk on Thursday, saying he had nearly broken down in tears when the former president professed ignorance of apartheid atrocities.
Tutu, chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told a news conference that de Klerk's answers to commission questioning during a public hearing on Wednesday had been unacceptable.

"When you say you didn't know -- and I know, I am among many who went to this government with information about the sort of things we are now investigating...there was almost an avalanche of information -- to say you do not know, I find that difficult," Tutu said, his voice breaking.
"I can't accept for someone to say the claims that people were being tortured, that those were being used as misleading propaganda.... I, I've got to say, I was close to tears."
In his testimony on Wednesday de Klerk, who was education minister for the most of the 1980s and became president in 1989, told the commission that murder and torture were never government policy.

He said he had not been aware of the atrocities now being revealed by the truth commission, describing them as aberrations, and renewed his apology for the suffering which apartheid caused. De Klerk began dismantling the policy in 1990.
But Tutu said de Klerk's attitude to human rights abuses meant that his apology counted for nothing.

"Mr de Klerk made a very impassioned apology, a handsome apology. For me...to make the apology and then to negate it, I feel sorry for him," said Tutu, a leading anti-apartheid campaigner during the 1980s.
"They believed in this policy, but it's a policy that we accept brought about all this suffering.
"It didn't happen haphazardly. It was a policy that killed people. Not by accident, deliberately. It was planned," Tutu said.

He cited the example of systematic police harassment at the many funerals of black activists where he had presided. "It seems to me extraordinary that there should be 'aberrations' that are so uniform."
Tutu said he had personally told de Klerk during the early 1990s of witness accounts of police taking part in massacres apparently intended to destabilise black communities.
"I told him. I told him things.... And when I told him, they said we were vilifying the police."
Asked why he had not challenged de Klerk during the testimony on Wednesday, Tutu said:
"I couldn't guarantee that I wouldn't cry. I was devastated.... I'm so deeply committed to this country, I hope these people would just hear us, hear the cry."
Tutu's deputy chairman Alex Boraine, describing the state of emergency declared in South Africa during the 1980s as a licence to kill, said the commission had hoped for a fuller accounting.
"We feel yesterday (Wednesday) was wasted," he said.
Tutu rejected accusations by de Klerk's National Party that the commission had shown bias in favour of the African National Party in the way it handled submissions from the two sides this week.

Asked on Thursday about the ANC's assertion to the commission that it had never regarded the rival Inkatha Freedom Party of Mangosuthu Buthelezi as a military target, Tutu said only that the commission would make its own assessment.
About 15,000 blacks died during a decade of feuding between Inkatha and the ANC which erupted in the mid-1980s.
